background.note: A woman who can do magic in the old British stories about King Arthur. In this series she is kind and loves books.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded. For once he agreed with her.
paragraphs.simple: Jack nodded. This time, which was not usual, he agreed with Annie.

paragraphs.context: “But what about our mission?” said Annie. “What
paragraphs.simple: Annie asked about their important job. What about helping Morgan?

paragraphs.context: “We’ll come back,” said Jack. “We’ll have to
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they would come back. Next time they would be ready.

paragraphs.context: “That way,” said Jack, pointing in the opposite
paragraphs.mainIdea: They do not know the way.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said "That way" and pointed the other way from Annie.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry, Peanut.” Annie started to pat the
paragraphs.simple: Annie told Peanut not to worry and started to stroke her. But then she stopped.

paragraphs.context: Annie placed the mouse on the leafy forest
paragraphs.simple: Annie put the mouse on the forest floor, which was covered with leaves. She asked Peanut to take them to the tree house.

paragraphs.context: “There!” said Jack. He pointed to leaves rustling
paragraphs.simple: Jack pointed to leaves on the ground that were making a soft sound.

paragraphs.context: A streak of white passed over the leaves.
paragraphs.simple: Something white moved very fast over the leaves.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie followed the moving leaves. The
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie followed the leaves that were moving. Something white came and went again.

paragraphs.context: The forest floor was still. There was no
paragraphs.simple: Nothing moved on the forest floor. They could not see Peanut anywhere.

paragraphs.context: Jack glanced around. Annie was standing on the
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked around quickly. Annie was on the other side of a tree near them, pointing up.

paragraphs.context: “She saved us again,” said Annie. “She’s running
paragraphs.simple: Annie said Peanut saved them again. Peanut was climbing up the ladder alone.

paragraphs.context: They followed Peanut all the way up to
paragraphs.mainIdea: They climb up to the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: They followed Peanut up the ladder, all the way to the top of the rain forest.

paragraphs.context: Peanut was sitting on a stack of books.
paragraphs.simple: Peanut was sitting on a pile of books.

paragraphs.context: Annie patted Peanut’s little head. “Thanks,” she said
paragraphs.simple: Annie gently touched Peanut’s little head and quietly said thank you.

paragraphs.context: Annie began searching for the Pennsylvania book—the book
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie looks for the book that takes them home.
paragraphs.simple: Annie started to look for the Pennsylvania book. That book always took them home.

background.note: A state in the east of the USA. Jack and Annie’s town, Frog Creek, is in Pennsylvania.

paragraphs.context: He had wanted to take lots of notes
paragraphs.simple: Jack wanted to write lots of notes in the rain forest. But up to now he had only written a little.

paragraphs.context: Annie was right. The Pennsylvania book was nowhere
paragraphs.simple: Annie was right. They could not see the Pennsylvania book anywhere.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up. The monkey was sitting in
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked up. The monkey was in the window. His head was a little to one side, and he seemed to be smiling at them.

paragraphs.context: “No! Don’t throw it!” said Jack. He ducked.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid of the fruit.
paragraphs.simple: Jack shouted "Don’t throw it!" and moved his head down quickly.

paragraphs.context: He held it out to Annie. He moved
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkey gives Annie the fruit.
paragraphs.simple: The monkey held the fruit out to Annie. He moved his lips like he was trying to talk.

paragraphs.context: Annie stared into the monkey’s eyes. He moved
paragraphs.simple: Annie looked into the monkey’s eyes. He moved his lips again.

paragraphs.context: “One of the special things we’re supposed to
paragraphs.mainIdea: The fruit is the special thing.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said the fruit was one of the special things they had to find to free Morgan from the magic.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded. Now he remembered. The ninja master
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack remembers the ninja master’s words.
paragraphs.simple: Jack nodded. He remembered what the ninja master said: they could not find the Pennsylvania book until they found the thing they were looking for.

background.note: The leader of the ninjas in book 5. He gave the children the moonstone.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie looked at him. He was
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie looked at the monkey. He was clapping his hands.

paragraphs.context: The monkey was gone. He had vanished below
paragraphs.simple: The monkey had left. He went down below the treetops and they could not see him.

paragraphs.context: A happy screech came from the mysterious world
paragraphs.simple: A happy screech came from the strange world down below.

paragraphs.context: Jack sighed. He picked up his notebook again.
paragraphs.simple: Jack let out a long breath. He picked up his notebook again and looked at what he wrote.

paragraphs.context: Jack put away his notebook. Annie picked up
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are ready to go home.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his notebook back in its place. Annie picked up the Pennsylvania book.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was still.
paragraphs.simple: Then nothing moved.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. Peanut was on the
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his eyes. Peanut was on the shelf at the bottom of the tree house window.

paragraphs.context: “Here it is!” he said. He read out
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds the fruit in the book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said "Here it is!" and read the words so Annie could hear.

paragraphs.context: “The mango has a sweet taste like that
paragraphs.simple: The book said a mango is sweet and tastes like a peach.

background.note: A tropical fruit. Mangoes first came from South Asia, but now they grow in many hot places, like Brazil.

paragraphs.context: “Mango? Hmmm,” said Annie. She brought the fruit
paragraphs.simple: Annie said "Mango?" and brought the fruit near her mouth.

paragraphs.context: Jack placed the mango on the M carved
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack puts the mango with the moonstone.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put the mango on the M that was cut into the floor, next to the clear moonstone.

paragraphs.context: “Moonstone … mango,” whispered Annie. It sounded like
paragraphs.mainIdea: The two names sound like magic.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said "Moonstone ... mango" quietly. It sounded like magic words.

paragraphs.context: “We’re halfway there,” said Jack. “Two more to
paragraphs.mainIdea: They have found half the things.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they had found half of the things. Two more were left.

paragraphs.context: “Then we can free you, Morgan!” Annie called
paragraphs.simple: Annie said they would free Morgan soon. She said it like Morgan was close by and could hear.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, brother,” said Jack. He needed more proof
paragraphs.simple: Jack said "Oh, brother." He needed more facts to believe it.
paragraphs.tone: Jack likes facts. He thinks Annie’s feelings are not enough.

paragraphs.context: “You know, that monkey was never being mean,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie said the monkey was never trying to be unkind. He just wanted to give them the mango.

paragraphs.context: “I know. Actually, nothing was being mean,” said
paragraphs.simple: Jack agreed. Nothing was trying to be unkind. The army ants were just walking, because that is what army ants do.

paragraphs.context: “The jaguar was just taking care of her
paragraphs.mainIdea: The jaguar was being a good mother.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said the jaguar was only looking after her baby.

paragraphs.context: Annie shuddered. “I still don’t love bugs,” she
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie still does not like bugs.
paragraphs.simple: Annie shook a little. She said she still did not love bugs.

paragraphs.context: “You don’t have to love them,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said she did not have to love them. If she did not touch them, they would not trouble her.

paragraphs.context: In fact, that’s true about the whole rain
paragraphs.mainIdea: We should not hurt the rain forest.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought this was true for the whole rain forest. Everyone should not cut it down or change it.
paragraphs.tone: This is the big idea of the book: we should protect the rain forest.

paragraphs.context: “Who cares if the bugs don’t have names?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bugs do not need names.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said quietly that it did not matter if the bugs had no names. They know who they are.
paragraphs.tone: Jack has changed. At the start he wanted to name new bugs. Now he thinks they are fine without names.

paragraphs.context: They started walking up their street. It was
paragraphs.simple: They started walking up their street. The evening sun made it look golden.

paragraphs.context: “Race you!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said "Race you!" — she wanted to see who could run home first.

paragraphs.context: “Safe!” they shouted together, tagging their front door.
paragraphs.simple: They touched their front door at the same time and shouted "Safe!"
paragraphs.tone: "Safe!" is what children shout in games like tag when they reach "home". After a scary trip, they really are safe now.

sentences.context: Now Jack and Annie are about to set out in search of the second thing … in Afternoon on the Amazon.
sentences.simple: Now Jack and Annie are going to start a trip very soon. They will look for the second special thing in this book, Afternoon on the Amazon.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie are about to set out.

parts.job: What they will do very soon.
parts.meaning: are going to start a trip very soon

parts.text: in search of the second thing
parts.meaning: to look for the second special thing

parts.job: Where you can read about it: the name of this book.
parts.meaning: in this book, Afternoon on the Amazon.

sentences.grammar: "Be about to" means "be going to do it very soon". "Set out" means "start a trip". "In search of" means "looking for".

sentences.context: In old Japan, Peanut had helped them when they’d gotten lost.
sentences.simple: When they were lost in Japan long ago, Peanut helped them.

parts.meaning: In Japan, long ago (in the last book),
Peanut helped them before this story
at the time when they did not know the way.

sentences.grammar: "Had helped" and "had gotten" are the past perfect. They tell about something that happened before the main story. "Gotten" is American English for "got".

sentences.context: Plus, the rain forests are being cut down
sentences.simple: Also, people are cutting down the rain forests now.
sentences.main: The rain forests are being cut down.

parts.meaning: are having their trees cut down by people (now).

sentences.grammar: "Are being cut down" = "people are cutting them down now". "Be being + past participle" is the passive for an action that is going on now. We don’t say who does it.

sentences.context: Thick treetops, often over 150 feet in the air, make up the top layer.
sentences.simple: The top level of the forest is made of thick treetops, which are often more than 150 feet high.
sentences.main: Thick treetops make up the top layer.

parts.text: often over 150 feet in the air,
parts.meaning: which are often more than 150 feet high,

sentences.grammar: The words between the two commas give extra information about the treetops. You can leave them out: "Thick treetops make up the top layer." "Make up" here means "form; be the parts of".

sentences.context: Below the canopy is the understory, then the forest floor.
sentences.simple: Under the canopy there is the understory, and under that is the forest floor.
sentences.main: The understory is below the canopy.

parts.job: The next thing in the list.
parts.meaning: and next comes the forest floor.

sentences.grammar: The usual order is "The understory is below the canopy." Here the place comes first and the verb comes before the subject. Books often do this to describe places from top to bottom.

sentences.context: The ladder seemed to fall between the branches of a giant tree.
sentences.simple: The ladder looked as if it went down between the branches of a very big tree.

parts.text: between the branches of a giant tree.
parts.meaning: between the branches of a very big tree.

sentences.grammar: "Seem to + verb" means "look like it does something". Jack is not sure, because he cannot see far. Here "fall" means "hang down", not "drop".

sentences.context: Now that they were out of the sun, it was cooler.
sentences.simple: Because they were not in the sun any more, it was cooler.

parts.text: Now that they were out of the sun,
parts.meaning: Because they were not in the sun any more,

sentences.grammar: "Now that ..." gives a reason that is new: "Now that I have a bike, I can ride to school." "Cooler" = more cool, less hot.

sentences.context: In the rain forest, many living creatures blend in with their surroundings.
sentences.simple: In the rain forest, many animals look like the things around them.
sentences.main: Creatures blend in with their surroundings.

parts.meaning: look so much like the things around them that you cannot see them easily.

sentences.grammar: "Blend in with" is one phrasal verb: read it as one idea. "Surroundings" is always plural.

sentences.context: The sound means that 30 million flesh-eating army ants are marching through the dead leaves.
sentences.simple: The sound tells you that 30 million meat-eating army ants are walking through the dead leaves.
sentences.main: The sound means that army ants are marching.

parts.meaning: that 30 million ants that eat meat

parts.text: are marching through the dead leaves.
parts.meaning: are walking together over the dead leaves.

sentences.grammar: "Mean that ..." = "tell you that ...". "Flesh-eating" is one adjective made of a noun + "-ing" verb, like "English-speaking" or "fast-moving".

sentences.context: The Amazon River stretches over 4,000 miles from the mountains of Peru, across Brazil, to the Atlantic Ocean.
sentences.simple: The Amazon River is more than 4,000 miles long. It goes from the mountains of Peru, through Brazil, to the Atlantic Ocean.
sentences.main: The Amazon River stretches over 4,000 miles.

parts.meaning: starting in the mountains of Peru,
and ending at the Atlantic Ocean.

sentences.grammar: "From A, across B, to C" shows a path from the start to the end. "Over" here means "more than", not "above".

sentences.context: The river basin contains over half of the rain forests in the world.
sentences.simple: More than half of all the rain forests in the world are in the land around this river.
sentences.main: The river basin contains over half of the rain forests.

parts.text: over half of the rain forests in the world.
parts.meaning: more than half of all the world’s rain forests.

sentences.context: But all he saw was a small brown monkey, hanging by its tail from a tree.
sentences.simple: But the only thing he saw was a small brown monkey. It was hanging from a tree by its tail.
sentences.main: All he saw was a monkey.

parts.job: The subject: "all he saw" = the only thing he saw.
parts.meaning: But the only thing he saw

parts.text: hanging by its tail from a tree.
parts.job: Describes the monkey: what it was doing.
parts.meaning: which was hanging from a tree by its tail.

sentences.grammar: "All I saw was ..." means "I saw only ...". The "-ing" part after the comma tells what the monkey was doing.

sentences.context: At night, they quietly bite their victims and suck their blood.
sentences.simple: At night, vampire bats quietly bite animals and drink their blood.
sentences.main: They bite their victims and suck their blood.

parts.meaning: the bats bite animals without making a sound

sentences.grammar: One subject ("they") does two things joined by "and": "bite" and "suck". The present simple is used for facts about animals.

sentences.context: He moved his lips as if he were trying to say something.
sentences.simple: He moved his lips like he wanted to talk.

parts.text: as if he were trying to say something.
parts.meaning: like he was trying to talk.

sentences.grammar: "As if" tells what something looks like, when it may not be true. After "as if", books often use "were" for all people: "as if he were ...".

sentences.context: The ninja master said they wouldn’t be able to find the Pennsylvania book until they had found what they were looking for.
sentences.simple: The ninja master told them: you will not find the Pennsylvania book before you find the thing you are looking for.

parts.text: they wouldn’t be able to find the Pennsylvania book
parts.meaning: that they could not find the Pennsylvania book

parts.text: until they had found what they were looking for.
parts.job: The condition: when it would be possible.
parts.meaning: before they found the thing they were looking for.

sentences.grammar: Reported speech moves the tenses back: "You won’t be able to" becomes "they wouldn’t be able to"; "you have found" becomes "they had found". "Not ... until" means "only after".

sentences.context: In fact, that’s true about the whole rain forest, Jack thought.
sentences.simple: Jack thought this was really true for all of the rain forest too.
sentences.main: That’s true about the whole rain forest.

parts.text: that’s true about the whole rain forest,
parts.meaning: this is true for all of the rain forest,

sentences.grammar: Thoughts can be written without quote marks: "..., Jack thought." "That" points back to what Jack just said: leave things alone and they won’t bother you.

catch up with.meaning: To reach someone who is in front of you, by going faster.
catch up with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take off.meaning: (1) To leave or run away quickly and suddenly. Birds and planes "take off" when they go up into the air. (2) To remove clothes or a bag from your body ("took off his backpack").
take off.example: Jack and Annie took off through the rain forest.
take off.usageNote: Very common. It also means a plane leaving the ground, or taking off your clothes.

oh brother.meaning: A thing you say when you think something is silly or annoying (informal, American English).
oh brother.usageNote: Informal spoken English. It has nothing to do with a real brother.

oh man.meaning: A thing you say when you are surprised, excited or worried (informal, American English).
oh man.usageNote: Informal spoken English. Jack says it a lot.

pick up.meaning: To take something in your hand and lift it. When the wind "picks up", it gets stronger.
pick up.example: Annie picked up the tiny lump.
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

turn into.meaning: To make something become something different.
turn into.example: Yesterday Annie had turned her sock into a bed for Peanut.
turn into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get lost.meaning: To not know where you are or how to get back.
get lost.example: Peanut had helped them when they’d gotten lost.
get lost.usageNote: A common phrase. "Gotten" is American English; British English says "got".

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: “I’d better find out what it is,” said Jack.
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

rain forest.meaning: A thick forest with very tall trees in a hot place where it rains a lot.
rain forest.example: On the cover were the words The Rain Forest.
rain forest.usageNote: A common phrase. It is also written "rainforest".

get it.meaning: To understand (informal). "I don’t get it" means "I don’t understand".

make sense.meaning: To be easy to understand; to seem right.
make sense.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

cut down.meaning: To cut a tree so that it falls to the ground.
cut down.example: the rain forests are being cut down
cut down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm or brave.
take a deep breath.example: Annie took a deep breath and slowly nodded.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

a sea of.meaning: A very large number or amount of something, spread over a wide area.
a sea of.example: They had landed in a sea of shiny green leaves.
a sea of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

make up.meaning: To be the parts that form something.
make up.example: Thick treetops, often over 150 feet in the air, make up the top layer.
make up.usageNote: A common phrase. It has other meanings too, like "to make up a story" (invent it).

keep going.example: We have to keep going, he thought.
keep going.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

blend in with.meaning: To look so much like the things around you that you are hard to see.
blend in with.example: many living creatures blend in with their surroundings
blend in with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

tons of.example: There’re tons of creatures down here.

come alive.meaning: To suddenly become full of life, movement and sound.
come alive.example: Just then the silent forest came alive.
come alive.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

army ant.meaning: A kind of ant that moves in a huge group and eats other small animals.
army ant.example: The sound means that 30 million flesh-eating army ants are marching through the dead leaves.
army ant.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

push your way.meaning: To move through something by pushing it out of your way.
push your way.example: They pushed their way through the bushes.
push your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in the distance.example: He listened to the crackling sound in the distance.
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

dig out.meaning: To make a hole or empty space inside something by digging or cutting.
dig out.example: The inside of the log was dug out.
dig out.usageNote: You only need to understand it here.

look this up.meaning: To find a piece of information in a book or on the internet ("look up" + the thing you want to know).
look this up.example: “We’d better look this up,” said Jack.
look this up.usageNote: A common phrase. Careful: "Jack looked up" (with nothing after it) just means he raised his eyes.

flip through.meaning: To turn the pages of a book quickly.
flip through.example: He pulled the rain forest book out of his backpack and flipped through it.
flip through.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

watch it.meaning: Be careful! (said quickly to warn someone).
watch it.usageNote: Informal. It can also sound like a warning when someone is angry.

stare in horror.meaning: To look at something for a long time because you are very shocked and afraid.
stare in horror.example: He and Annie stared in horror at each other.
stare in horror.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

make a face.meaning: To move your face in a funny or unhappy way to show you do not like something.
make a face.example: “What now?” said Annie, making a face.
make a face.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

hurt someone’s feelings.meaning: To make someone sad by saying or doing something unkind.
hurt someone’s feelings.example: “I think I hurt his feelings,” said Annie.
hurt someone’s feelings.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

who cares.meaning: (informal) It does not matter; I am not interested.
who cares.usageNote: Informal. It can sound rude, so be careful.

uh oh.meaning: A thing you say when you see that something bad may happen.

go on.meaning: To happen. "What’s going on?" means "What is happening?"
go on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

all the way.example: The monkey pulled the canoe all the way to the bank of the river.
all the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

act like.meaning: To work as something, or to behave in the same way as it.
act like.example: But the treetops acted like a huge umbrella.
act like.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

for their lives.meaning: "Run for your life" means run as fast as you can to escape danger.
for their lives.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

get away.meaning: To escape from someone or something.
get away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

catch your breath.meaning: To rest until you can breathe normally again after running.
catch your breath.example: Jack and Annie stopped running and caught their breath.
catch your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take care of.meaning: To look after someone or something.
take care of.example: “The jaguar was just taking care of her baby,” said Jack.
take care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

of course.meaning: Here: as you would expect; it is clear that.
of course.example: Of course, jaguars are fast, too, Jack thought.
of course.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

for once.meaning: This one time, which is not usual.
for once.example: For once he agreed with her.
for once.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

all by herself.example: She’s running up the ladder. All by herself.
all by herself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

so far.example: But all he’d written so far was:
so far.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

nowhere in sight.example: The Pennsylvania book was nowhere in sight.
nowhere in sight.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

be supposed to.meaning: Should; to have to do something because you were told or because it is the rule.
be supposed to.example: One of the special things we’re supposed to find for Morgan
be supposed to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as if.meaning: In a way that shows something, though it is not said or not true.
as if.example: He moved his lips as if he were trying to say something.
as if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

put away.meaning: To put something back in the place where it is kept.
put away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

out loud.meaning: So that other people can hear.
out loud.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

we’re halfway there.meaning: We have done half of the job.
we’re halfway there.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

two more to go.meaning: Two more are left to do.
two more to go.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

leave alone.meaning: To not touch, change or bother someone or something.
leave alone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

race you.meaning: (said to a friend) Let’s run and see who gets there first!

break the silence.meaning: To make a sound when it was very quiet.
break the silence.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in fact.meaning: Really; the truth is. It is used to add something stronger.
in fact.example: In fact, that’s true about the whole rain forest, Jack thought.
in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

about to.meaning: Going to do something very soon.
about to.example: I was about to call you.
about to.usageNote: Very common. "I was about to call you" means "I was going to call you right then".

set out.example: They set out early in the morning.
set out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in search of.example: They went in search of food.
in search of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

under a spell.example: The princess was under a spell.
under a spell.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

along the way.meaning: While you are going somewhere or doing something.
along the way.example: There will be more help along the way.
along the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.
